course.title: Drawing and Visual Art Fundamentals
course.description: Learn to see accurately and draw what you see: line, proportion, form, perspective, value, light, colour and composition, with practice on paper.
course.audience: A curious adult with little or no drawing training who is willing to practise on paper with a pencil and a sketchbook. Needs school-level proportion and angle; no artistic talent assumed.

paragraphs: Most people who say they can't draw have never been taught where to look. A drawing goes wrong less often because the hand is clumsy than because the eye has been replaced by what we know: we draw an almond for an eye and four straight legs for a chair, and then wonder why the picture looks off. This course starts by putting that habit aside and drawing the shapes, spaces and proportions that are really in front of you.

From there we build up the pieces that make a picture look solid. We make controlled lines, construct forms from boxes and cylinders, and work out how a circle becomes an ellipse. We place the horizon and the vanishing points that govern perspective, and we calculate how large a figure should be at a given distance. Then we turn to light: the value scale, the bands of light on a form, the length of a shadow, and the marks that build tone. Last come colour and composition, followed by a full study that ties them together.

You'll need a pencil, a sketchbook and a ruler. Each lesson explains one set of ideas, asks you to check your understanding with questions that have exact answers, and sets a short exercise to do on paper. The exercises are rated by you against criteria in the lesson, because the best judge of a drawing is you looking at it.
outcomes: You'll be able to draw what is in front of you by comparing shapes, angles and proportions rather than naming objects.
You'll be able to make controlled lines, vary their weight on purpose, and construct basic forms and ellipses.
You'll be able to place objects in one-point and two-point perspective with a consistent horizon.
You'll be able to simplify a scene into a few values and model a form with light and shadow.
You'll be able to describe colour by hue, value and chroma, and use complements and temperature.
You'll be able to compose a picture with thumbnails and judge your own work against clear criteria.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Geometry: Shape and Space.

modules.title: Seeing and marks
modules.description: Looking for shapes and proportions, making confident lines, and building forms.

modules.title: Space and perspective
modules.description: Cues for depth, and the rules of one- and two-point perspective.

modules.title: Light and value
modules.description: Value as the structure of a picture, and how light models a form.

modules.title: Colour and composition
modules.description: Describing and combining colour, arranging a picture, and finishing a study.

concepts.title: Drawing from symbols
concepts.summary: When you draw what you know instead of what you see, you draw a symbol, such as an eye as an almond shape.

concepts.title: Shape
concepts.summary: A shape is a flat area with an outline, such as a triangle or an irregular patch.

concepts.title: Negative space
concepts.summary: Negative space is the shape of the empty area around and between objects, and drawing it checks the positive shapes.

concepts.title: Comparative measurement
concepts.summary: Comparing one length or angle to another, instead of judging it in isolation, is more accurate.

concepts.title: Perceptual illusion
concepts.summary: An illusion shows that the eye's impression can differ from measurement, which is why drawing uses comparison.

concepts.title: Contour
concepts.summary: A contour line follows the edge of a form, and cross-contour lines wrap around it to show its surface.

concepts.title: Gesture
concepts.summary: A gesture drawing captures the movement and direction of a subject in a few quick lines.

concepts.title: Line weight
concepts.summary: Heavier lines suggest shadow, nearness or emphasis, and lighter lines suggest distance or light.

concepts.title: Ghosting
concepts.summary: Ghosting is moving the pen over the paper without marking, to rehearse the line before drawing it in one confident stroke.

concepts.title: Arm motion
concepts.summary: Long lines come from the shoulder and elbow, because wrist drawing makes short, curved strokes.

concepts.title: Proportion
concepts.summary: Proportion is the relation between sizes, such as width to height, and it is kept when the ratio is kept.

concepts.title: Sighting
concepts.summary: Sighting holds a pencil at arm's length and compares one length with another, using one of them as the unit.

concepts.title: Scale factor
concepts.summary: Scale factor is the ratio of new size to old, applied to every length.

concepts.title: Grid method
concepts.summary: The grid method draws a grid on the reference and a grid of equal proportions on the paper, and copies the lines square by square.

concepts.title: Head units
concepts.summary: Figure proportions are often counted in heads: teaching canons use about 7.5 or 8 heads for an adult.

concepts.title: Form
concepts.summary: Form is the three-dimensional volume of an object, as opposed to its flat shape.

concepts.title: Basic forms
concepts.summary: Most objects can be started as a sphere, box, cylinder or cone, adjusted afterward.

concepts.title: Ellipse
concepts.summary: A circle seen at an angle appears as an ellipse, with a long axis (major) and a short axis (minor).

concepts.title: Degree of an ellipse
concepts.summary: The ratio of minor to major axis equals the sine of the angle between line of sight and the circle's plane, so it rounds as you look more directly at it.

concepts.title: Minor axis rule
concepts.summary: The minor axis of the ellipse of a cylinder's end lies along the cylinder's axis.

concepts.title: Overlap
concepts.summary: An object that covers part of another appears nearer.

concepts.title: Size and distance
concepts.summary: The apparent size of an object is inversely proportional to its distance, so twice as far looks half the size.

concepts.title: Vertical placement
concepts.summary: On level ground, things farther away sit higher up the picture, nearer the horizon.

concepts.title: Atmospheric perspective
concepts.summary: Distant objects look paler, bluer and lower in contrast because of haze.

concepts.title: Texture gradient
concepts.summary: Repeated texture, such as paving stones, looks finer and closer together with distance.

concepts.title: Horizon line
concepts.summary: The horizon line is the viewer's eye level, and every object whose eye height matches yours has it pass through its eyes.

concepts.title: Vanishing point
concepts.summary: A vanishing point is where parallel lines receding from the viewer appear to meet, on the horizon line.

concepts.title: Orthogonals
concepts.summary: Orthogonals are the receding lines, drawn toward the vanishing point.

concepts.title: One-point perspective
concepts.summary: In one-point perspective a face of the box is parallel to the picture plane, so its horizontals stay horizontal, its verticals stay vertical and only the depth lines converge.

concepts.title: Above and below the horizon
concepts.summary: A box above the horizon shows its underside, a box below shows its top, and one crossing it shows neither.

concepts.title: Two-point perspective
concepts.summary: In two-point perspective neither face is parallel to the picture plane, so the horizontal edges recede to two points on the horizon while verticals stay vertical.

concepts.title: Direction pairs
concepts.summary: Each vanishing point belongs to one set of parallel edges, so a box has one for its width edges and one for its depth edges.

concepts.title: Three-point perspective
concepts.summary: When you look steeply up or down, the vertical edges also converge to a third vanishing point above or below.

concepts.title: Distance and distortion
concepts.summary: Vanishing points that are close together make extreme foreshortening; further apart looks more natural.

concepts.title: Foreshortening
concepts.summary: Foreshortening is the compression of a form that points toward the viewer.

concepts.title: Value
concepts.summary: Value is how light or dark an area is, separate from its hue.

concepts.title: Value scale
concepts.summary: A value scale is a sequence of equal steps from white to black, often with five or nine steps.

concepts.title: Simplifying values
concepts.summary: A picture reads clearly when its values are grouped into a few masses, such as three to five.

concepts.title: Local value and lighting
concepts.summary: Local value is the object's own lightness; lighting then makes it lighter or darker.

concepts.title: Luminance and grey
concepts.summary: Colour is converted to grey with weights that reflect the eye's sensitivity: roughly 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B for screens (Rec. 709 luma).

concepts.title: Terminator
concepts.summary: The terminator is the line where a form turns from light into shadow.

concepts.title: Core shadow
concepts.summary: The core shadow is the darkest band on the form, just inside the terminator, not at the edge, because reflected light brightens the edge.

concepts.title: Parts of light
concepts.summary: On a lit sphere the parts are the highlight, light, halftone, core shadow and reflected light, with a cast shadow on the ground.

concepts.title: Cast shadow
concepts.summary: A cast shadow falls opposite the light direction and is darkest near the object.

concepts.title: Shadow length
concepts.summary: For a vertical object of height h in sunlight at elevation angle a, shadow length is h / tan a.

concepts.title: Edge types
concepts.summary: A hard edge is a sharp change in value, a soft edge a gradual one, and a lost edge fades into the background.

concepts.title: Hatching
concepts.summary: Hatching is a set of parallel lines whose spacing and pressure set the tone.

concepts.title: Cross-hatching
concepts.summary: Cross-hatching layers sets of lines at different angles to darken a tone.

concepts.title: Pencil grades
concepts.summary: H pencils are harder and lighter and B pencils softer and darker, with HB in the middle.

concepts.title: Hatching coverage
concepts.summary: Lines of width w at spacing p cover about w/p of the paper.

concepts.title: Hue, value and chroma
concepts.summary: Hue is the colour family, value its lightness and chroma its purity or intensity (Munsell's three dimensions).

concepts.title: Additive and subtractive mixing
concepts.summary: Light mixes additively from red, green and blue, and pigment subtractively from cyan, magenta and yellow.

concepts.title: Complementary colours
concepts.summary: Complementary colours sit opposite on a wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet in the traditional painter's wheel.

concepts.title: Colour temperature
concepts.summary: Reds, oranges and yellows are warm, blues and greens cool, and temperature is relative to neighbours.

concepts.title: Simultaneous contrast
concepts.summary: A colour looks different next to another: a grey patch looks warmer beside blue, and chroma intensifies next to its complement.

concepts.title: Thumbnail
concepts.summary: A thumbnail is a small, quick sketch used to test arrangements before the final drawing.

concepts.title: Focal point
concepts.summary: The focal point is where the picture is meant to be read first, emphasised by contrast, detail or position.

concepts.title: Rule of thirds
concepts.summary: Dividing the picture into thirds both ways gives four intersections where a focal point often sits (named by John Thomas Smith in 1797).

concepts.title: Leading lines
concepts.summary: Lines in the picture can lead the eye towards the focal point.

concepts.title: Balance
concepts.summary: Balance distributes visual weight so that a large light shape can balance a small dark one.

concepts.title: Process
concepts.summary: A study goes from large to small: placement, shapes and proportions, values, edges, then details.

concepts.title: Time budget
concepts.summary: A fixed time is divided so the large decisions get the most time and the details the least.

concepts.title: Stepping back
concepts.summary: Looking at the drawing from a distance, or in a mirror, shows errors that closeness hides.

concepts.title: Criteria
concepts.summary: A self-review scores proportion, value structure, form, edges, composition and process.

concepts.title: Practice habit
concepts.summary: Short, regular practice with a clear target improves drawing more than occasional long sessions.

lessons.title: Seeing shapes, not things

steps.headline: When we draw what we know instead of what we see, we draw a symbol.

lead.text: Try drawing an eye. Most of us produce an almond with a circle in the middle and a dot inside the circle, the same few curves we have been making since childhood. A real eye rarely looks like that. The upper lid cuts across the top of the iris, the white may hardly show at all, and the whole shape changes the moment the head turns.

The almond is what we *know* about an eye, boiled down to a few lines that are quick to make and easy to recognise. A picture made from stored knowledge like that is a **symbol**, and the same thing happens with a chair, which we draw as a seat on four straight legs even when the chair in front of us shows two legs, a slanted seat and a back that hides part of itself.

afterFigure.text: Drawing well starts by putting the stored version aside. What is in front of you is a set of flat patches, each with an edge, and the figure at the top of this lesson shows how a chair looks when you stop naming its parts and look at the patches instead.

lead.text: Before we say anything about how the eye judges length, look at the two lines in the figure. A ruler laid along line A reads 100 units from one end to the other. Decide what it will read when you lay it along line B.

reveal.text: The ruler reads 100 on both lines. The next screen shows why they look different and what to do about it.

diagram.alt: Two horizontal lines, the upper with arrowhead ends and the lower with fin ends. A ruler reads 100 units along the upper line.
diagram.caption: Line A is measured at 100 units. Decide what the same ruler reads along line B.

steps.headline: The eye judges a length by its surroundings, so a first impression of length can be wrong.

lead.text: The figure is the Müller-Lyer illusion, named after the German sociologist Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, who published it in 1889. Both lines have a shaft of the same length. The one with arrowhead ends tends to look shorter and the one with outward-turned fins tends to look longer, and the effect stays even after you have measured them, because the eye does not report a length in isolation. It reports the length *in its setting*, and the ends belong to the setting.

Why does that matter for drawing? When you judge a proportion by looking at a single feature, your impression is being pulled around by whatever surrounds it. A **perceptual illusion** is exactly this: an impression that disagrees with measurement. We can't switch the effect off, so we do what the guides in the second view do and put one length directly against another.

afterFigure.text: That habit is the core of the whole course. Rather than asking how long something is, we ask how it compares with something beside it, and we check the comparison against a straight edge, a pencil held at arm's length, or another part of the same drawing.

diagram.alt: Two horizontal lines of the same length, the upper with arrowhead ends and the lower with fin ends. In the second view two dashed vertical guides run through the ends of both lines and show they are equal.
diagram.caption: The two lines are exactly the same length. Switch to the second view to see the guides.

steps.headline: A shape is a flat patch with an outline, and the empty space around objects has shapes too.

lead.text: We call any flat area with an edge a **shape**, whether it's a triangle or a ragged patch with no name. A mug seen from the side is a tall shape for the body and a smaller one for the handle, and between the handle and the body there's a third, the hole you could put a finger through. Nothing is drawn there, yet it has an outline and a size like the other two.

The empty area around and between objects is called **negative space**, and the objects themselves are the positive shapes. Negative space is useful because we have no stored symbol for it. Nobody has a habit of drawing the gap under a chair seat, so when we draw that gap we can only draw what we see.

afterFigure.text: The check works in both directions. If the gap between the chair's legs looks wrong on your page, one of the legs is in the wrong place, even though you were never looking at the legs. You can find an error in the drawing by comparing it with the spaces.

diagram.alt: A mug in side view with the hole inside its handle shaded. The second view labels the body and the hole as two shapes.
diagram.caption: The hole in the handle is empty space, but it has an outline and a size like any other shape.

lead.text: Go back to the chair at the top of this lesson, in its second view. The three shaded regions are the same kind of thing, and drawers have a standard name for the empty area around and between solid objects.

reveal.text: Spaces can be drawn first, and the objects then appear between them without ever being named.

steps.headline: Compare one length with another and name the result as a ratio, since a ratio survives any change of size.

lead.text: The question to ask of any object is whether it is longer than it is tall, and by how much. Take the mug. Its body is 10 cm tall and 8 cm wide, so it is taller than it is wide, and if we divide the height into five equal parts, the width comes to four of them. We say the height and width are in the ratio **5 to 4**.

That answer is more useful than either number alone. It says the same thing about a mug drawn 5 cm tall or 50 cm tall, and it gives your eye one question to ask the paper: if I call the height five parts, are there four across? Check 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8, and 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8, so the two descriptions agree.

afterFigure.text: Using the longer side as the unit is a convenience, since the other side comes out as a fraction of it. A habit worth building is to pick the biggest dimension first, give it a size of your own choosing, and measure everything else against it.

diagram.alt: A mug in side view, 200 units tall and 160 wide, with a ruler of equal parts. The first view counts 5 parts up the height, the second counts 4 parts across the width.
diagram.caption: Take one part as 40 units. The body is 5 parts tall and 4 parts wide, so its height and width are in the ratio 5 to 4.

steps.headline: Find how many parts wide a mug is when its height is 5 parts and its real dimensions are 10 cm by 8 cm.

workedSteps.text: Write the real height and width.
Divide the width by the height, which gives the width as a fraction of the height.
Multiply the fraction by 5, the number of parts we gave the height. Work out how many parts the width is.

lead.text: Now a different object. A book stands on a shelf, 24 cm tall and 18 cm wide. As with the mug, call its height 4 parts and work out how wide it must be drawn, in the same parts.

reveal.text: Three parts across for four up is a ratio of 4 to 3. The same arithmetic worked for the mug, and it will work for any object whose proportions you can measure.

steps.headline: Start with the large shapes and spaces, so the small ones are placed against something already right.

lead.text: Beginners tend to start with the part they find most interesting, which is usually a small detail such as an eye or the handle of the mug, and then build outward. The trouble is that each new part is placed by eye against the last one, and the small errors add up, so the far side of the drawing ends up too big or too far off.

Starting large reverses that. First put down the overall outline of the object, as one or two big shapes and the proportion between them, and check that with a ratio like 5 to 4. Then divide those shapes into smaller ones, each placed inside something already settled. Drawing talent turns out to be mostly this way of looking, and it can be practised like any other skill.

afterFigure.text: The details you drew at the end are the same ones you would have drawn at the start. They now have somewhere correct to sit.

lead.text: You are about to draw a chair that stands in front of you, and you want its legs, seat and back to stay in proportion with one another. Think about which starting point gives every later mark something already right to be placed against.

reveal.text: Starting with the overall outline means every detail is placed inside it, so the biggest errors are caught before the smallest marks are made.

lessons.orientation: Look at an object as shapes and spaces, compare lengths by eye, and see why impressions mislead.
lessons.nextAction: Make controlled straight and curved lines from the shoulder and choose a line weight on purpose.

blocks.text: Draw a chair from memory: a seat, four legs, a back. Everyone's chair looks about the same, and yours probably looks like the one you drew at six. Now look at a real chair across the room. Its legs overlap, the seat is a slanted sliver, and the shape under the seat between the legs is nothing like the straight-sided rectangle you drew.

What you drew was a list of parts you know. What you see is a set of flat shapes with edges, and the gaps between them are shapes too. The figure shows the same chair both ways, and the second way is the one an accurate drawing starts from.

diagram.alt: A chair seen from the front, drawn as flat shapes. In the first view its parts are shaded: two uprights, a top rail, a middle rail and a seat. In the second view the three gaps between those parts are shaded instead.
diagram.caption: The same chair twice. Use the buttons to switch between its parts and the three empty shapes between them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to see an object as shapes and spaces, compare its lengths as a ratio, and say why a first impression of length can be wrong.
intro.whyItMatters: Accurate drawing begins with accurate looking, and the habits here make every later lesson easier.

recap.keyIdea: Draw the shapes and spaces you see, and judge every length by comparing it with another.

blocks.text: A symbol is what we know of an object, and an accurate drawing is made of what we see: flat shapes with edges, plus the negative space between them. The eye judges each length in its setting, as the Müller-Lyer lines showed, so we compare one length with another and keep the result as a ratio such as 5 to 4.
Start with the large shapes and the spaces between them, and place the smaller ones against what is already right.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts a pencil to paper, with the controlled lines and varied weights that carry what you now see.

lessons.title: Line and mark

steps.headline: A confident line is rehearsed in the air and then drawn once, which is the whole technique of ghosting.

lead.text: Look at the two ways of joining the same pair of dots in the figure at the top. The hesitant version looks careful, because it is made of many small corrections, but the corrections pile up into a blur, and the eye can no longer tell which stroke was meant. The single stroke makes one claim about where the line goes, and if the claim is wrong the error is plain to see and easy to fix on the next try.

The way to get one good stroke is to rehearse it first. **Ghosting** means moving the pen over the paper without marking, from the start point to the end point, again and again, until the motion is smooth. Then, with the same motion and the same speed, you let the pen touch down and draw the line once. The Drawabox course teaches the same order of work: plan the line, rehearse it, and then execute it in one go.

afterFigure.text: Rehearsing is not the same as hesitating. In ghosting all the doubt is spent in the air, where it costs nothing, and the mark on the paper is made with the confidence of a line you have already drawn three times.

steps.headline: A long line comes from the shoulder and elbow, because a pen pivoting about the wrist can only draw a tight curve.

lead.text: Why do lines drawn with the fingers and wrist bow? A pen that pivots about a point draws part of a circle centred on that point, and the closer the pivot, the sharper the curve. Take a line 15 cm long, drawn by a pen 8 cm from the pivot, as it is when the hand turns about the wrist. The pen traces an arc of radius 8 cm through the two dots, and we can find how far the middle of the arc rises above the straight line.

The pivot is at distance 8 cm from each dot and sits level with the midpoint of the line, so the right triangle of the pivot, the midpoint of the chord and one dot has hypotenuse 8 and one leg 7.5, half of 15. Its other leg is √(8² − 7.5²) = √7.75 ≈ 2.78 cm, which is how far the pivot sits from the chord. The arc therefore rises 8 − 2.78 ≈ 5.2 cm above it. With the pivot 50 cm away, as it is when the whole arm swings from the shoulder, the same calculation gives √(50² − 7.5²) ≈ 49.43, so the rise is only 0.57 cm.

afterFigure.text: That is the reason to draw long lines from the **shoulder**, with the elbow and wrist held loose and the pen sliding on the paper's surface. The rule for any line is that the farther the pivot, the straighter the arc, and a short line is simply an arc you cannot see.

diagram.alt: A 15 centimetre straight chord drawn to scale, with the arc a pen makes when it swings about a pivot. With a pivot 8 centimetres away the arc bows well above the chord. With a pivot 50 centimetres away it barely leaves the chord.
diagram.caption: A 15 cm line drawn to scale at 20 units per centimetre. The orange segment is how far the middle of the arc rises above the straight chord.

lead.text: Use the same method on a new line. The pen is 10 cm from its pivot, and you draw a straight 16 cm line between two dots. Work out how far the middle of the arc rises above the straight chord.

reveal.text: Half of 16 is 8, so the pivot sits 6 cm from the chord, and the arc rises 10 − 6 = 4 cm. The method is the same for any radius and line length.

steps.headline: Line weight is how heavy a line is, and varying it on purpose shows where things overlap, touch and turn into shadow.

lead.text: Both mugs in the figure have the same shape and the same edges, yet the one on the right looks like it stands on a table. The only difference is **line weight**: the thickness and darkness of the lines. When all lines are equal, as on the left, nothing in the drawing is said to be nearer, darker or more important than anything else, so the whole thing reads as a flat diagram.

A few habits make weight work. Draw heavier lines where the object meets the surface it stands on and on the side turned away from the light, since both places are in shadow. Draw them heavier too where one form overlaps another, such as where the handle joins the body, to say which one is in front. Keep lines thin on the lit side and in the distance. Controlled weight comes from the same one-stroke habit, because pressing harder on the pencil while moving is easier when the motion is already settled.

afterFigure.text: Weight is a decision made for each line, so an even outline is not a neutral choice. It is a choice to say nothing about where the light falls.

diagram.alt: The same mug drawn twice. In the first drawing every line has the same weight. In the second the left edge is thin and the right edge, base and handle are heavier.
diagram.caption: The same mug with the light coming from the left. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Imagine a mug on a table, lit from the upper left, with its handle on the right. Before you draw the outline, decide where a heavier line would do the most good.

reveal.text: The base touches the table and the right side is turned from the light, so both are in shadow and carry the heavier lines.

steps.headline: A contour line follows the edge of a form, and cross-contour lines wrap around it to show how its surface turns.

lead.text: Many people hear "contour drawing" and think "outline". An outline does follow the edge of a form, and we call a line that does so a **contour**, but it tells you only where the form ends. The left side of the figure shows a cup this way: a flat shape that could as well be a cut-out of card.

Add curved lines that go *across* the form, as if the cup were wrapped in string, and the shape becomes round. We call these **cross-contour** lines. Each one is a slice through the form, a cross-section seen at an angle, so it curves one way if we look down on it and the other if we look up. A pen that follows the whole outline and then these curves is describing the surface, and that is the sense of contour that matters when we get to form in a later lesson.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the curves in the figure all bow the same way. On a cup seen from above they bow downward, and drawing every one with the same curvature is what keeps the form looking like one object.

diagram.alt: A cup drawn as a cylinder. The first case shows only its outline, the top ellipse and the sides. The second adds three curved lines that wrap around the cup, which show that its surface is round.
diagram.caption: The outline says where the edge is. The curved lines across the body say how the surface turns.

lead.text: Every form has an edge where it ends and the background begins. Name the kind of line that follows it.

reveal.text: The same word names a way of drawing in which you move the pen along an edge as your eye travels along it.

steps.headline: A gesture drawing records the movement and direction of a subject in a few fast strokes, with no detail.

lead.text: A **gesture** drawing is the opposite of a careful contour. In half a minute there is no time for edges, so the strokes have to follow the *direction* things move: the curve of the back, the angle of the thigh, the line of the shin. In the figure there are five strokes for a seated figure, made in the order numbered, and each is one stroke from the shoulder.

Why bother with something so rough? Because a gesture fixes the largest decision in a drawing, the way the whole subject is arranged, before any smaller one is made. If the gesture is wrong, a perfect eye will not rescue the drawing, and if it is right, the details have something to hang from. Speed is the tool here, since a drawing made in thirty seconds cannot become fussy.

diagram.alt: A seated figure drawn with five strokes: the curve of the back, a head circle, a thigh, a shin and a line for the arm. The numbers give the order the strokes were made in.
diagram.caption: A gesture drawing of someone sitting. Each stroke follows a direction of movement, and none draws a detail.

steps.headline: Draw a straight line between two dots 15 cm apart, using ghosting.

workedSteps.text: Mark the two dots, 15 cm apart, and hold the pen just above the first dot.
Ghost the line three times, with the pen moving over the paper without touching it, from the shoulder, and without stopping at the end.
On the fourth pass, with the same speed and the same motion, let the pen touch down and draw the line once.
Lift the pen at the end dot and look at the result. If the line misses a dot, do not correct it with a second stroke. Ghost and draw a new one beside it.

lead.text: Now draw a longer line, 30 cm, from the shoulder with a pivot 50 cm from the pen. Work out how far the middle of the arc would rise above a straight chord, and compare it with the 0.57 cm of the 15 cm line.

reveal.text: A line twice as long rises about four times as far, 2.3 cm against 0.57 cm, so longer lines need a more committed arm than short ones.

lessons.orientation: Make controlled lines from the shoulder, vary line weight on purpose, and tell contour from gesture.
lessons.nextAction: Measure proportions by sighting along a pencil, and scale a drawing with a grid.

blocks.text: Put two dots on a page, 15 cm apart, and join them. Most of us make one cautious stroke, see that it sags, and go over it again, and again. After the sixth pass the page holds a thick grey smear that is close to the right place and clearly the work of someone who didn't trust their hand.

A single stroke, made at an even speed, looks quite different. It is either right or wrong, and the difference between the two is easy to read, which is exactly what you need to improve. What makes one stroke straight and another bowed, and what a line can say by being heavy or light, is a matter of the arm and the pencil, and both are easy to learn.

diagram.alt: Two ways of joining the same two dots. The first case shows six hesitant, wobbling strokes that blur together. The second shows one straight stroke.
diagram.caption: The same two dots, joined two ways. Use the buttons to compare.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to draw a straight line in one stroke from the shoulder, choose heavier or lighter lines on purpose, and tell contour from gesture.
intro.whyItMatters: Every drawing is made of lines, so a controlled line improves everything built on it.

recap.keyIdea: Rehearse a line with ghosting, draw it once from the shoulder, and choose its weight to show shadow, contact and overlap.

blocks.text: A pen swinging from the wrist draws an arc, which is why a long line is drawn from the shoulder after being rehearsed in the air. Line weight carries information too: heavier where a form meets a surface, overlaps another or turns away from the light, and lighter where it is lit.
A contour line follows an edge, cross-contour lines wrap around the form to show its surface, and a gesture drawing uses a few fast strokes to catch the movement.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses a pencil as a measuring tool, so that the shapes you now draw with one stroke are also in proportion.

lessons.title: Proportion and measuring

steps.headline: Sighting means holding a pencil at arm's length and using one length as the unit for measuring the others.

lead.text: How do you find out that a drawing is too wide? By measuring the object the same way you measure the drawing. Hold your pencil out at arm's length, with the arm straight and the elbow locked, and close one eye. Slide your thumb along the pencil until the top of the pencil and your thumb cover the length you want to use as the unit, such as the width of the window in the figure, and then, without moving your thumb or bending your arm, carry that same length across to the other dimension and see how often it fits.

The locked arm matters. When you bend your arm, the pencil comes closer to your eye and appears larger, so the length your thumb marks is no longer the length you marked a moment ago. In the figure the window's width fits once up its side and leaves a third over, so we say its height is **1⅓ units**, and its shape is 4 to 3. Unit lengths are a form of the comparison we met in the first lesson, now made with a tool that doesn't change.

afterFigure.text: Use the longest dimension of whatever you are drawing as the unit where you can, so that every other length is a fraction of it. Then write the fractions down, since a number on the page is easier to check than a memory.

diagram.alt: A window in front view, 3 units wide and 4 tall in shape. In the first view a pencil with a thumb mark is held across the width, and the mark records the width as one unit. In the second view the same length is carried up the side and fits one and a third times.
diagram.caption: The width is the unit. The same pencil length carried up the height fits once, with a third of a unit left over, so the height is 1⅓ units.

cases.label: Mark the unit

cases.label: Carry it up

lead.text: Suppose that while you are sighting a window you bend your arm a little for the second measurement. Think about what happens to the pencil as it comes toward your face, and what that does to the length your thumb marks.

reveal.text: Bending the arm changes the distance from your eye to the pencil, and a closer pencil covers more of the scene, which is why the arm must stay straight.

steps.headline: A scale factor is the ratio of new size to old size, and one factor must be applied to every length.

lead.text: Take a block 9 cm wide and 12 cm tall, and suppose it has to be drawn 8 cm tall. The drawing is smaller, and the number that says how much smaller is the **scale factor**, the new size divided by the old: 8 ÷ 12 = ⅔. If the drawing is to keep the shape of the block, the width must be multiplied by the same factor, so it comes to ⅔ × 9 = 6 cm. The new rectangle is 6 by 8, and its ratio is 3 to 4, the same as 9 to 12.

The second view shows what happens when only one length is scaled. A drawing 9 by 8 has the right height and the old width, so it is squashed, and nothing about it looks wrong until it is laid beside the original. The rule is that a scale factor applies to *every* length in the drawing, the sides of the whole and the smallest detail alike.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the factor does not depend on what the object is. It depends only on the ratio of one length you chose, 12 cm and 8 cm, and it is then applied to the others, which is how a mug can become a postage-stamp drawing without changing shape.

diagram.alt: A reference rectangle 9 by 12 next to two drawings at the same units. The first drawing is 6 by 8, with both sides scaled by two thirds, and has the same shape. The second is 9 by 8, with only the height scaled, and looks squashed.
diagram.caption: Both drawings are 8 cm tall. Only the first uses the same factor for the width.

lead.text: Use the same two steps on a new object. It is 15 cm wide and 20 cm tall, and you will draw it 12 cm tall. Find the scale factor first, then apply it to the width.

reveal.text: The factor is 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6, and 0.6 × 15 = 9, so the drawing is 9 cm wide and 12 cm tall, the same 3 to 4 shape as the object.

steps.headline: Scale a tile 28 cm wide and 21 cm tall to a drawing 6 cm tall.

workedSteps.text: The new height is 6 cm and the old height is 21 cm, so the scale factor is their ratio.
Apply the same factor to the width, 28 cm. Work out the width of the drawing.

steps.headline: The grid method rules the reference and the paper into the same number of squares, and copies what is in each square.

lead.text: Sighting is good for a few lengths, but for a complicated outline we can hand the scaling to a grid. Rule the reference into squares, say 2 cm each, and rule the paper into the same number of squares of a different size, say 3 cm. Then copy the drawing one square at a time, putting each line where it crosses the sides of its square. Because the squares are copies of each other, the copy keeps the proportion of the original wherever you look.

The scale factor here is 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5, and it applies to every length, so the house in the figure that is 8 cm wide on the 2 cm grid is 12 cm wide on the 3 cm grid. The grid does not make a drawing correct, but it turns one hard judgement over the whole picture into many easy ones, such as where a line crosses the third square from the left.

afterFigure.text: The squares must stay squares. If the new grid is 3 cm wide and 4 cm tall, we have scaled the two directions by different factors, which is the squashing from the previous screen again.

diagram.alt: A house outline drawn on a four by four grid. In the first view the squares are 2 centimetres and the house is 8 centimetres wide. In the second the squares are 3 centimetres and the same outline, passing through the same grid points, is 12 centimetres wide.
diagram.caption: The outline passes through the same grid points in both. Each square stays a square, so every length is multiplied by 1.5.

lead.text: A reference is ruled into 2 cm squares and your paper into 5 cm squares. Apply the scale factor to a line on the reference that is 8 cm long.

reveal.text: The factor is 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5, so an 8 cm line becomes 20 cm on the paper, crossing four reference squares and four paper squares.

steps.headline: Figures are measured in heads, with the height of one head as the unit, and teaching canons use about 7.5 or 8 heads for an adult.

lead.text: The human figure is the one subject that comes with a unit built in. Drawers often use the height of the head, from chin to top of the skull, as the unit for the whole body, and we call these multiples **head units**. A teaching canon is a convention that says how many head units an adult is: some teachers use 7.5 and others use 8. They are rules of thumb for drawing, since real people vary around them, and a source that uses one is not wrong about the other.

The sums are scale-factor sums. Draw the head 3 cm high, and an eight-head figure is 8 × 3 = 24 cm tall, which tells you where to put the feet before you draw the body. With the canon of 7.5, the same 3 cm head gives 22.5 cm. This is the same idea as before, with the head as the unit, and it lets you fix the size of a figure on the page from one measurement.

diagram.alt: A column of equal boxes, each one head tall, stacked eight high in the first view and seven and a half in the second. A bracket gives the total in heads.
diagram.caption: Two teaching canons for an adult. They are conventions for drawing, and real people vary around them.

lead.text: You have chosen the 7.5-head canon, and your figure will have a head 4 cm tall. Use the head as the unit to work out how tall the whole figure will be.

reveal.text: The figure is 7.5 × 4 = 30 cm tall, so you know the feet go 30 cm below the top of the head before you have drawn anything else.

lead.text: Now work the head unit backwards. You have a space on the page 36 cm tall and want the 7.5-head figure to fill it exactly. Work out how tall the head must be drawn.

reveal.text: Dividing the height by the number of heads gives the unit: 36 ÷ 7.5 = 4.8 cm. Fixing the unit first and building up from it is how a figure is placed on a page.

lessons.orientation: Measure proportions by sighting, scale with a factor or a grid, and use head units for figures.
lessons.nextAction: Build forms from simple shapes and draw the ellipse that describes a circle in space.

blocks.text: A card is 9 cm wide and 12 cm tall, and you need it on your page about 8 cm tall. It's easy to draw something 8 cm by 8 cm, since the card looks a little squarish, and the drawing will look off in a way you may not be able to name. Lay the card and the drawing side by side and the cause is plain: the card is three quarters as wide as it is tall, and the drawing is as wide as it is tall.
A feeling that something is wrong can be turned into a measurement, and a measurement can be turned into a correction. The pencil and the ratio we met in the last lesson are enough to do that.

diagram.alt: A card 9 centimetres wide and 12 centimetres tall, and a square drawing of it 8 centimetres on each side, both at the same scale. The card has width divided by height of 0.75 and the drawing has 1.
diagram.caption: At the same scale, the drawing is visibly too wide. Width divided by height gives 0.75 for the card and 1 for the drawing.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to measure a proportion by sighting, scale a drawing by a factor, and use a grid or head units to place the parts.
intro.whyItMatters: A drawing in the right proportion reads as the object, and one in the wrong proportion reads as a different one.

recap.keyIdea: Pick one length as the unit, find the scale factor, and apply the same factor to every length.

blocks.text: Sighting uses a pencil held at arm's length with a locked elbow, so that one length can be carried across to another, and the result is a ratio such as 4 to 3. The scale factor is the new size divided by the old, and the grid method applies it in small steps by ruling the reference and the paper into squares of different sizes.
For a figure the head is the unit, with teaching canons of 7.5 or 8 heads for an adult, so one head height fixes the height of the whole figure.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson builds solid forms out of simple shapes, which asks a new question: how is a circle drawn when we look at it from the side?

lessons.title: Form and ellipses

steps.headline: A form is the solid volume of an object, and most forms can be started from a sphere, a box, a cylinder or a cone.

lead.text: In the first lesson a shape was a flat patch with an outline. An object in the room is more than that, since it has depth and fills space, and we call its three-dimensional volume its **form**. A plate seen from the front gives us a circle as a shape, and the same plate has a form, a flat cylinder, which is why it turns into something different when we tilt it.

The useful discovery is that most objects begin as one of four **basic forms**. A ball starts as a sphere, a book as a box, a can as a cylinder and a funnel as a cone, and a more complicated object such as a kettle is a few of them joined and trimmed. Draw the basic form first and the proportions and the direction of its surfaces are settled before any detail is added, a habit we already used when we started with the large shapes.

afterFigure.text: The figure puts each flat shape beside its form. The change is the same in all four: a line that curves or slants across the shape, showing us the form's depth.

diagram.alt: Four flat shapes, a circle, square, triangle and rectangle, and next to them four solid forms, a sphere, box, cylinder and cone, each drawn with curved or slanted lines that show its depth.
diagram.caption: The solids are the flat shapes given depth. Use the buttons to compare.

cases.label: Flat shapes
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360"><circle class="f-sunken s-ink w2" cx="110" cy="200" r="50"/><rect class="f-sunken s-ink w2" x="200" y="150" width="100" height="100" rx="0"/><polygon class="f-sunken s-ink w2" points="345,250 435,250 390,150"/><rect class="f-sunken s-ink w2" x="500" y="145" width="60" height="110" rx="0"/><text class="t" x="110" y="290" text-anchor="middle">circle</text><text class="t" x="250" y="290" text-anchor="middle">square</text><text class="t" x="390" y="290" text-anchor="middle">triangle</text><text class="t" x="530" y="290" text-anchor="middle">rectangle</text></svg>

lead.text: The word for the solid volume of an object, as opposed to the flat patch it makes in a drawing, is the one this lesson is built on.

reveal.text: Form is what we draw with, in cross-sections and ellipses, and what the next screens work out.

steps.headline: A circle seen at an angle appears as an ellipse whose short axis is the diameter times the sine of the angle between the line of sight and the circle's plane.

lead.text: Every cup has a circular rim, and every wheel a circular rim, and every circle looks different depending on where we stand. At eye level a rim is a flat line, from straight above it is a circle, and in between it is an **ellipse**, a smooth closed curve with a long axis, the **major axis**, and a short one, the **minor axis**. The major axis always keeps the full diameter, because it runs across the tilt, where the circle is not foreshortened.

The minor axis is shorter by a definite amount. The angle between the line of sight and the plane of the circle is α, and the minor axis is the diameter times sin α, as the figure shows: the disc seen edge-on is a line, and the width it covers across the line of sight is that line's length times sin α. For a 10 cm circle seen at 30° to its plane the minor axis is 10 × sin 30° = 5 cm, at 45° it is about 7.07 cm, and at 90° it is 10 cm, a circle.

afterFigure.text: Both ends of an ellipse are smooth and rounded. People who draw an ellipse with pointed ends are drawing a lemon, and people who flatten the near side are drawing a bowl with a lid. The near and far edges of the circle are both curves.

diagram.alt: Left, a side view of a flat circular disc as a tilted line seen edge-on, with parallel lines of sight coming straight down. The width the viewer sees is the length of the line's shadow below it. Right, the ellipse that results, with its major axis of 120 units and its minor axis shown.
diagram.caption: The disc's width across the tilt is the diameter times the sine of the angle between the line of sight and the disc. Use the buttons for three angles.

cases.label: 90° to the plane

lead.text: Use the relation on a plate 24 cm across. You look at it with your line of sight 30° above its plane. Work out how long its minor axis is.

reveal.text: sin 30° is one half, so the minor axis is half the plate's diameter, 12 cm, while the major axis is still 24 cm.

steps.headline: The ellipse opens as the line of sight steepens, so its ratio of minor to major axis tells us the viewing angle.

lead.text: Compare the four ellipses in the figure. All four have the same width, and they differ in how open they are, from a thin sliver to a circle. The ratio of the minor axis to the major axis is sin α, so the ellipse's **degree of openness** carries a number: a ratio of 0.5 means the line of sight is 30° from the plane, a ratio of 0.25 means about 14.5°, and a ratio of 1 means we look straight down the axis and see a circle.

This is why one object has several ellipses. A can seen from slightly above has an ellipse at its top and another at its base, and the one nearer eye level is the narrower, because we are looking at it at a smaller angle. The base lies farther below eye level, so it is rounder. A common error is drawing the two ends with the same ellipse, which makes the can look like a flat stencil.

afterFigure.text: The rule to keep is that the ellipse is narrowest at eye level and rounds as it gets farther above or below it.

diagram.alt: Four ellipses with the same width of 100 units, labelled A to D. Their heights are a quarter, a half, three quarters and all of the width.
diagram.caption: Same width, different heights. The second view gives each height as a fraction of the width.

lead.text: The four ellipses A to D in the figure have the same major axis of 120 units, with minor axes of 30, 60, 90 and 120 units. Think about which one belongs to a circle seen with the line of sight 30° above its plane.

reveal.text: Ellipse B is half as tall as it is wide, and sin 30° is 0.5. Ellipse A is about 14.5°, C about 48.6° and D is the view from straight above.

diagram.alt: Four ellipses with the same width of 100 units, labelled A to D, from narrow to round.
diagram.caption: The four ellipses all share one width. They differ in how open they are.

steps.headline: The minor axis of the ellipse at the end of a cylinder lies along the cylinder's own axis, wherever the cylinder points.

lead.text: Draw a line down the middle of a cylinder, from the centre of one end to the centre of the other. This is its axis. The ellipse at each end has its long direction at right angles to the axis, because a circle at the end of a cylinder is perpendicular to it, and so its short direction lies *along* the axis. We call this the **minor axis rule**.

The rule holds when the cylinder is upright, where the minor axes are vertical, and when it lies on its side, where they are horizontal, and when it tilts at any angle. A common mistake is to treat the minor axis as horizontal on the page, which turns a tilted can into a wobbling one. Instead, find the cylinder's axis first, then draw each ellipse with its short direction along that line.

afterFigure.text: The last view repeats the point about eye level for a can seen from slightly above, with the nearer-eye-level top ellipse narrower than the base.

diagram.alt: A cylinder shown upright, lying on its side, tilted, and as a can seen from slightly above. A dashed line marks the cylinder's axis, and it runs along the short axis of the ellipse at each end.
diagram.caption: The dashed axis passes through the middle of each end ellipse along its short direction. The dotted lines are the long axes.

cases.label: Seen from above

steps.headline: Work out the viewing angle from an ellipse with a major axis of 20 cm and a minor axis of 10 cm.

workedSteps.text: The ratio of the minor axis to the major axis is the sine of the angle.
We know that sin 30° = 0.5, so the line of sight is 30° above the plane of the circle.
Check the other way: a circle 20 cm across seen at 30° has a minor axis of 20 × sin 30°. Work out that length.

lead.text: A cylinder lies on its side on a table, so its own axis points horizontally across your view. Decide which direction the short axis of the ellipse at its end takes.

reveal.text: The short axis lies along the cylinder's axis, so for a cylinder on its side it is horizontal, and the long axis is vertical.

lead.text: Now a different angle. A 10 cm circle is seen with the line of sight 45° above its plane. You need sin 45°, which is about 0.7071, to work out the minor axis.

reveal.text: At 45° the minor axis is about 7.07 cm. That sits between the 5 cm of 30° and the 10 cm of 90°, as it should.

lessons.orientation: Start objects from basic forms, and draw ellipses with the right opening and the right axis.
lessons.nextAction: Use overlap, size, position and haze as cues for depth.

blocks.text: Look at the rim of a cup from the side, at eye level, and it is a straight line. Lift your head and the line opens into a thin ellipse. Look straight down into the cup and the ellipse becomes a circle. The rim never changed, so what changed, and how much?

The answer is a number we can work out, and the same number tells you how to draw every wheel, bowl and can you will ever meet. The figure shows the rim in three positions with the same width, and only the height changes.

diagram.alt: The rim of a cup drawn at three viewing angles with the same width. At eye level it is a flat line. From 30 degrees above it is an ellipse half as tall as it is wide. From straight above it is a circle.
diagram.caption: One circular rim, three viewpoints. The width stays at 120 units, and only the height changes.

cases.label: Level with the rim
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360"><line class="s-ink w3" x1="260" y1="170" x2="380" y2="170" /><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="290" text-anchor="middle">Line of sight 0° above the rim plane</text><text class="t-small t-muted" x="320" y="318" text-anchor="middle">Width 120, height 0</text></svg>

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to build objects from basic forms, say how open an ellipse should be for a given viewing angle, and place an ellipse correctly on a cylinder.
intro.whyItMatters: Circles are everywhere in objects, and drawing them as ellipses of the right shape is what makes a form look solid.

recap.keyIdea: A circle in space is an ellipse whose minor axis is the diameter times the sine of the viewing angle, and that axis lies along the cylinder's axis.

blocks.text: A form is the solid volume an object fills, and most objects begin as a sphere, box, cylinder or cone. A circle seen at an angle is an ellipse with its major axis equal to the diameter and its minor axis equal to the diameter times sin α, where α is the angle between the line of sight and the circle's plane.
On a cylinder, the minor axis of each end ellipse follows the cylinder's own axis, and the ellipse nearer eye level is the narrower one.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how a flat drawing makes things seem near or far, using overlap, size, position and haze.

lessons.title: Cues for depth

steps.headline: When one object covers part of another, we read the covering object as nearer, and this needs no line construction.

lead.text: The figure builds a landscape in layers, starting with three identical trees that sit side by side in a row. The picture is flat because nothing in it says which tree is nearer. Slide the middle tree across the other two so that it hides a piece of each, and you read it at once as being in front. This is the cue called **overlap**, and it is the simplest and strongest of the depth cues.

Many people think that perspective means converging lines and a vanishing point, and we will meet those in the next two lessons. Overlap, size, placement, texture and haze all give depth without a single construction line, and a drawing that uses several of them at once, as the later views of the figure do, looks deeper than one that relies on any single cue.

afterFigure.text: Overlap tells us the order of things but not how far apart they are, which is why it is usually combined with size and placement.

diagram.alt: Five versions of three trees. The first has three identical trees side by side and no sense of depth. The second overlaps them. The third also makes the back trees smaller. The fourth also raises the smaller trees toward a horizon. The fifth also draws the distant trees paler and thinner.
diagram.caption: Each view adds one cue to the previous one. Step through them to watch the depth appear.

lead.text: In the second view the middle tree hides part of the two beside it. Name the depth cue at work there.

reveal.text: Overlap gives only the order of the objects, so it is combined with cues that say how far apart they are.

lead.text: A figure 2 m tall stands 10 m from you, and you draw it 4 cm tall on the page. It then walks to a point 20 m away, twice as far. Predict how tall, in centimetres, you would draw it now.

reveal.text: The drawn height halves to 2 cm. The next screen gives the rule behind that, and shows what happens at 40 m.

steps.headline: The drawn height of an object is inversely proportional to its distance, so twice as far looks half as tall.

lead.text: Objects that are the same real size look smaller the farther away they are, and the rule is exact. Drawn height is **inversely proportional** to distance, meaning that the product of the two stays the same: 4 cm × 10 m is 40, so at 20 m the height is 40 ÷ 20 = 2 cm and at 40 m it is 40 ÷ 40 = 1 cm. Each doubling of the distance halves the height, which is the steep curve in the second view.

The rule is about height, and it is easy to apply to the wrong quantity. If a figure is half as tall, it is also half as wide, so the area it covers on the page is a half times a half, a *quarter* of what it was. When you scale a figure to show it farther away, scale both its height and its width by the same factor, as in the lesson on proportion.

afterFigure.text: The curve falls fastest close to you and slowly far away, which is why a row of nearby objects changes size sharply from one to the next and a row at the horizon changes hardly at all.

diagram.alt: Left, a figure 2 metres tall drawn at 4, 2 and 1 centimetres for distances of 10, 20 and 40 metres. The second view plots drawn height against distance, a curve that falls steeply at first and then flattens, through the points 4 centimetres at 10 metres, 2 at 20 and 1 at 40.
diagram.caption: Each time the distance doubles, the drawn height halves. The curve is drawn height = 40 ÷ distance.

cases.label: Three figures
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360"><line class="s-soft w2" x1="60" y1="300" x2="580" y2="300" /><rect class="f-accent-soft s-accent w2" x="128.4" y="180" width="43.2" height="120" rx="0"/><text class="t-small" x="150" y="324" text-anchor="middle">10 m</text><text class="t-small t-accent" x="150" y="170" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><rect class="f-accent-soft s-accent w2" x="309.2" y="240" width="21.6" height="60" rx="0"/><text class="t-small" x="320" y="324" text-anchor="middle">20 m</text><text class="t-small t-accent" x="320" y="230" text-anchor="middle">2 cm</text><rect class="f-accent-soft s-accent w2" x="484.6" y="270" width="10.8" height="30" rx="0"/><text class="t-small" x="490" y="324" text-anchor="middle">40 m</text><text class="t-small t-accent" x="490" y="260" text-anchor="middle">1 cm</text><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="52" text-anchor="middle">The same 2 m figure at three distances</text></svg>

lead.text: A fence post is drawn 6 cm tall when it is 15 m from you. Use the fact that drawn height times distance stays the same, and find the height at which you would draw an identical post 45 m away.

reveal.text: The product is 6 × 15 = 90, so at 45 m the height is 90 ÷ 45 = 2 cm. Tripling the distance divides the height by three.

steps.headline: Draw a 2 m figure at 25 m, knowing it is drawn 4 cm tall at 10 m.

workedSteps.text: Multiply the drawn height by the distance to find the constant for this figure and this page.
The drawn height at any distance is this constant divided by that distance.
Put in the new distance of 25 m and work out the height, in cm.

steps.headline: On level ground, far things sit higher up the picture and their textures shrink, and both effects come from the same ground plane.

lead.text: Stand on a flat field and look at three identical people at different distances. The farthest has the smallest figure, and the soles of its feet sit *highest* in your view, closest to the horizon, where the ground seems to meet the sky. We call this **vertical placement**: on level ground the lower an object's base is in the picture, the nearer it is. The first view shows it with the figures from before.

The ground carries the same message in its texture. Paving stones that are all the same size look larger and farther apart near you, and finer and closer together as they recede, so a surface covered with a repeating pattern shows its distance in the rate of change of the pattern. We call this a **texture gradient**, and in the second view the rows of stones become shorter and narrower toward the horizon.

afterFigure.text: Notice that both cues need a ground plane. A figure floating in a blank sky gives no placement cue, and a scene with no repeating pattern gives no texture cue.

diagram.alt: Two views of level ground. In the first, three identical figures stand at increasing distances, and the farther ones are drawn smaller and higher, nearer the horizon. In the second, rows of paving stones get shorter and narrower toward the horizon.
diagram.caption: Both effects come from the same ground plane: far things are small and sit near the horizon.

cases.label: Placement
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360"><line class="s-warn w1 dash" x1="40" y1="70" x2="600" y2="70" /><text class="t-small t-warn" x="44" y="62" text-anchor="start">horizon</text><rect class="f-accent-soft s-accent w2" x="247.4" y="150" width="25.2" height="70" rx="0"/><rect class="f-accent-soft s-accent w2" x="313.7" y="110" width="12.6" height="35" rx="0"/><rect class="f-accent-soft s-accent w2" x="436.9" y="90" width="6.3" height="17.5" rx="0"/><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="340" text-anchor="middle">On level ground, farther figures stand higher</text></svg>

lead.text: Think about a flat square sign. It stands at some distance, and then you move it twice as far away. Its height halves, and so does its width. Work out what fraction of its first area it now covers in your view.

reveal.text: The area falls to a quarter, because both height and width were halved. It is a common mistake to halve the area only.

steps.headline: Distant things look paler, bluer and softer in haze, so a drawing lightens and softens each layer as it recedes.

lead.text: A mountain range seen across a valley is a pale shape, and the range behind it is paler still. The air between you and the mountains is not perfectly clear, so it scatters light, and each extra stretch of air lightens and blurs the surface behind it. We call this **atmospheric perspective**: distant objects lose contrast, show less detail and shift toward the colour of the air, which is usually a pale blue.

In a drawing, the effect is the one in the first view: each range is lighter, with a thinner outline, than the one in front of it. The second view leaves the haze out, and the layers look like stage flats cut from the same board. The rule is *loss of contrast*, not always *lighter*, because in a dark scene such as a night forest the air is dark and the distant trees melt into it, becoming no brighter than before and a little darker than the sky behind them.

diagram.alt: Three ranges of hills overlapping one another. In the first view the farthest is palest with the thinnest outline, and the nearest is darkest with the heaviest outline. In the second view all three are drawn with the same dark tone and line, and they look like cut-out layers.
diagram.caption: Haze lightens and softens the distant ranges. The second view leaves it out.

lead.text: Distant mountains drawn paler, bluer and with less contrast than the nearer ones all illustrate one of the depth cues. Choose it.

reveal.text: The effect comes from the air between us and the object, which is why it is named after the atmosphere.

lead.text: A drawing of a cobbled street makes the stones near the viewer large and widely spaced, and the stones near the end of the street small and closely packed. Name the cue that this uses.

reveal.text: The cue works with a surface that carries a repeating pattern, which is why a street, a field of corn and a tiled floor all show it.

lessons.orientation: Name the cues for depth, and calculate drawn size from distance.
lessons.nextAction: Place the horizon line and one vanishing point, and construct a box in one-point perspective.

blocks.text: Here is a picture of three identical trees in a row. It is flat, and no amount of staring at it will make one tree seem nearer than another. Now move the middle tree so that it hides part of each of its neighbours, and the picture changes entirely: the middle tree comes forward, and the other two step back, with no line anywhere that points to a vanishing point.

Overlap is one of five cues that tell the eye how far away things are, and the other four are size, placement on the ground, texture and haze. Each of them can be drawn with a pencil and nothing else, and the figure shows what each one adds.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the main cues for depth in a flat drawing and calculate how large a figure should be drawn at a given distance.
intro.whyItMatters: A drawing that uses several cues together looks deep before any perspective construction is used.

recap.keyIdea: Depth comes from overlap, size, placement, texture and haze, and drawn height is inversely proportional to distance.

blocks.text: A flat drawing can show depth by overlap, by making farther things smaller, by placing them nearer the horizon, by letting a texture get finer, and by lightening and softening them with haze. The size rule is exact: drawn height times distance stays constant, so twice the distance gives half the height and a quarter of the area.
Using two or more of these cues on each layer makes a picture deep without a single construction line.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson draws the lines that fix size and placement exactly: the horizon and a vanishing point, which together give one-point perspective.

lessons.title: One-point perspective

lead.text: You stand in a field with your eyes 1.6 m above the ground, and you look at a tree 20 m away. The horizon is the line at the level of your own eyes. Predict the height above the ground, in metres, at which the horizon line crosses the trunk of that tree.

reveal.text: The horizon crosses it at 1.6 m, and it would cross a tree 200 m away at the same 1.6 m. The next screen says why.

steps.headline: The horizon line is your eye level, and receding parallel lines appear to meet at a vanishing point on it.

lead.text: Stand at one end of a corridor and look along it. The two edges where the walls meet the floor, and the two where they meet the ceiling, all slope toward the middle of the far end, though we know they are parallel. In a drawing we show that by making them converge. The level line they meet on is the **horizon line**, which is your eye level, as the last question showed, and the point where they meet is the **vanishing point**.

Any line that runs straight away from you is an **orthogonal**, and all the orthogonals of one direction aim at the same vanishing point. The figure shows a corridor, and the second view continues its edges as dashed lines: they meet at a single point on the horizon, exactly in the middle of the far end. Leon Battista Alberti described this kind of construction in his treatise *On Painting* of 1435, in which he explains how to draw a floor of equal squares from a single point he called the centric point.

afterFigure.text: Be careful about where you put the horizon. It belongs at your eye level, not at the top of the picture because that is where the sky begins, and in a drawing of a room seen from a chair it may be near the bottom.

lead.text: The dashed lines of the corridor meet at one point on the horizon. Give the name of the point where receding parallel lines appear to meet.

reveal.text: Every set of parallel lines running in one direction has its own point, and in one-point perspective there is only one such set.

steps.headline: In one-point perspective a face of the box is parallel to the picture, so only the depth lines converge, and a box takes five steps.

lead.text: The simplest case is a box with one face turned squarely toward you. We call this **one-point perspective**, because only a single vanishing point is needed. The face turned toward us is parallel to the picture, so its horizontals stay horizontal and its verticals stay vertical, and it keeps its real shape: a square front face is drawn as a square. Only the edges running away from us converge.

Work through the figure. First draw the horizon and mark the vanishing point on it. Draw the front face as a square. Draw orthogonals from its corners to the point. Then pick how deep the box is by drawing the back face, a copy of the front face shrunk toward the vanishing point, and finally keep only the edges that you can see. For a box four metres from you and one metre deep, the back face is at five metres, so it is scaled by 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 toward the point, the same size rule as in the last lesson.

afterFigure.text: The scale factor does the work of the depth. A deeper box has a smaller back face, because it ends farther away.

diagram.alt: Five stages of drawing a box in one-point perspective: the horizon with a vanishing point, a square front face, dashed lines from its corners to the point, a smaller back face, and the finished box with only the visible edges drawn.
diagram.caption: Step through the five stages. The back face is the front face scaled toward the vanishing point by a factor of 0.8.

steps.headline: Find the height of the back face of a box whose front face is 90 units tall, with the front at 4 m and the back at 5 m.

workedSteps.text: The front face is 4 m away and the back face 5 m away, so the back face is scaled by the ratio of the distances.
Every length on the back face is the matching length on the front face times s, measured from the vanishing point, so the height scales by the same factor.
Work out the height of the back face.

lead.text: A new box has a front face 150 units tall at a distance of 6 m, and its back face is at 8 m. Find the scale factor for the back face first, and then the back face's height.

reveal.text: The factor is 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75, so the back face is 150 × 0.75 = 112.5 units tall. A longer box gives a smaller back face.

steps.headline: A box below the horizon shows its top, a box above it shows its underside, and a box crossing it shows neither.

lead.text: Which faces of a box can we see? That depends on where the box is relative to the horizon, which is your eye level. A box *below* your eyes, like a table, is seen from above, so its top shows. A box *above* your eyes, like a shelf, is seen from below, so its underside shows. A box that your eye level passes through shows neither top nor underside, only its front and, if it is off to one side of the vanishing point, one side face.

The sideways rule is the same. A box to the right of the vanishing point shows its left side, and a box to the left shows its right. In the figure all three boxes are the same, and moving the horizon changes what we see of them: with the horizon lowered, all three are above it and show undersides, and with it raised, all show tops.

afterFigure.text: This is a good reason to place the horizon first. It decides what every box in the picture shows, and putting it in later forces every box to be redrawn.

diagram.alt: Three identical boxes stacked at different heights to the right of the vanishing point. With the horizon at the middle, the upper box shows its underside, the middle one shows neither top nor underside, and the lower one shows its top. With the horizon lowered below all of them, all three show undersides. With it raised above all of them, all three show tops.
diagram.caption: Which faces you see depends only on whether the box is above or below the horizon.

lead.text: In a drawing you can see the underside of a box, and you can see no top. Think about where the viewer's eyes must be relative to the box.

reveal.text: The viewer looks up at a box that is above eye level, which is the case for a shelf or a high cupboard.

lead.text: A box stands to the left of the vanishing point, with its centre below the horizon. It shows its top. Decide which side face shows as well, the left or the right.

reveal.text: A box to the left of the vanishing point shows its right side, as the right side faces the middle of the picture. The top shows because it is below the horizon.

lessons.orientation: Place the horizon and a vanishing point, and construct a box in one-point perspective.
lessons.nextAction: Use two vanishing points to draw a box turned at an angle, and count the points in three kinds of perspective.

blocks.text: Look along a corridor and the edges of the floor, the walls and the ceiling all lean toward a single spot at the far end, even though you know they are parallel. If you lay a ruler along any of them in a photograph and extend it, they cross at one point, and that point is level with the camera.

That spot has a precise place in a drawing, and finding it first makes everything else follow, from the size of the far wall to which faces of a box you can see. The figure shows a corridor drawn from the middle, with the lines continued.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a horizon line and a vanishing point, build a box in one-point perspective, and say which faces of a box show.
intro.whyItMatters: A horizon and a point turn the guesswork of drawing depth into a construction you can check with a ruler.

recap.keyIdea: The horizon is your eye level, and the receding edges of a box aim at a vanishing point on it.

blocks.text: The horizon line is the viewer's eye level, and in one-point perspective every receding edge, called an orthogonal, runs toward a single vanishing point on it. A box is built by drawing the front face as a square, joining its corners to the point, and scaling the front face toward the point by the ratio of the distances to make the back face.
A box below the horizon shows its top, a box above it shows its underside, and a box on a side of the point shows the face that faces the centre of the picture.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns the box so that no face is parallel to the picture, which needs two vanishing points.

lessons.title: Two-point perspective

lead.text: Last lesson's box had one face parallel to the picture. Now turn the box a little about its vertical axis, so that none of its faces is parallel to the picture, and look at it from a level eye height. Its horizontal edges now run in two different directions. Predict how many vanishing points you need.

reveal.text: Two: one for each direction of horizontal edge. The next screen shows how they sit on the horizon, and what the vertical edges do.

steps.headline: In two-point perspective each direction of horizontal edge has its own vanishing point on the horizon, and the vertical edges stay vertical.

lead.text: When the cube is turned so that no face is parallel to the picture, the horizontal edges run in two directions, and we call the result **two-point perspective**. All the edges in one direction are parallel in space, so they meet at one point on the horizon, and all the edges in the other direction meet at a second point. In the figure the blue edges go to one point and the orange edges to the other, and the two points are on the *same* horizon line, since both are at the viewer's eye level.

The vertical edges stay vertical, since they are parallel to the picture. Drawers often think that every edge must lean, and that is a mistake we will deal with in a moment. Each vanishing point belongs to one **direction pair**, meaning the set of edges that share a direction. A cube has twelve edges, four in each of three directions, so four go to the left point, four to the right point, and four stay vertical.

afterFigure.text: A cube's edges are all the same length, but they are not evenly spaced in the drawing. The windows of a building shrink toward the vanishing point they recede to, as equal lengths do when the distance grows.

diagram.alt: A cube turned so that no face is parallel to the picture, seen from above its top, drawn in perspective. Edges in one direction are blue and edges in the other direction are orange, and the vertical edges stay vertical. In the first view the edges are continued as dashed lines, and each colour meets at its own point on the horizon.
diagram.caption: Blue edges go to one point and orange edges to the other. Both points lie on the same horizon, and the vertical edges stay vertical.
